subject: Anthropology
title: Decolonizing Anthropology
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Decolonizing Anthropology.

hook.text: Anthropology was born inside empires. It studied colonized peoples for colonial purposes. Can it be redeemed?

buildup.text: Decolonizing anthropology means confronting the discipline's role in colonialism and centering marginalized voices.

discovery.text: Indigenous scholars now write their own ethnographies, challenging outsider narratives that long defined them.

twist.text: Decolonization isn't just adding diverse voices. It means rethinking who gets to produce knowledge and for whom.

climax.text: Anthropology's future depends on becoming the discipline it claims to be — one that truly listens to all voices.

punchline.text: To study humanity, you must first respect it.

quiz.question: What does decolonizing anthropology mean?
options: Confronting colonial legacies and centering marginalized voices

details.summary: Decolonizing anthropology means confronting the discipline's colonial origins and transforming its practices to be more equitable. This includes sharing authority with research communities, centering indigenous knowledge, diversifying who becomes an anthropologist.
details.whyItMatters: Anthropology was born as a tool of colonialism, studying colonized peoples to aid governance. Decolonizing the discipline is essential for producing knowledge that serves all people rather than reproducing colonial power structures.
takeaways: Anthropology has colonial origins that shape its current practices
Decolonization means sharing authority with research communities
It requires centering indigenous knowledge and diversifying the field

faq.question: How was anthropology used as a tool of colonialism?
faq.answer: Colonial governments funded anthropological research to understand and manage colonized populations. Ethnographic knowledge helped identify power structures to manipulate, cultural practices to suppress, and divisions to exploit. The discipline provided intelligence for colonial administration.

faq.question: What does decolonized anthropology look like in practice?
faq.answer: Collaborative research where communities shape questions and benefit from results. Indigenous scholars leading research about their own cultures. Rejecting the assumption that Western analytical categories are universal. Publishing in local languages, not only English academic journals.
